notes.summary: Geometry is the biggest Advanced Maths topic: about 2 to 4 questions in Tier 1 and 3 to 5 in Tier 2. Almost every question uses a small set of facts about lines, triangles, circles and polygons. Learn the facts below, draw a rough figure for every question, and trust the given values because figures are not to scale.

concepts.title: Lines and angles
concepts.body:
Angles on a straight line add to 180° (a linear pair). Angles around a point add to 360°. When two lines cross, the vertically opposite angles are equal. Two angles adding to 90° are complementary; two adding to 180° are supplementary.

When a line (the transversal) cuts two parallel lines l and m, the figure gives these rules:

PairIn the figureRule
Corresponding angles1 and 5, 2 and 6, 3 and 7, 4 and 8Equal
Alternate interior angles4 and 6, 3 and 5Equal
Alternate exterior angles1 and 7, 2 and 8Equal
Co-interior angles (same side, between the lines)3 and 6, 4 and 5Add to 180°
Vertically opposite1 and 3, 2 and 4Equal

Example: if angle 3 = 70°, then angle 6 = 180° − 70° = 110° (co-interior) and angle 5 = 70° (alternate).

Trick for a bent "Z" shape between two parallel lines: the angle at the bend equals the sum of the two angles it makes with the parallel lines.

concepts.title: Triangle angle rules
concepts.body:
• The three angles of a triangle add to 180°.
  • Exterior angle = sum of the two opposite interior angles. If BC is extended to D, ∠ACD = ∠A + ∠B.
  • The larger side faces the larger angle. Equal sides face equal angles (isosceles triangle).
  • Triangle inequality: each side is less than the sum of the other two and more than their difference. Sides 3, 4 and 8 cannot make a triangle because 3 + 4 < 8.
  • Exterior angles of any triangle (one at each corner) add to 360°.

Angle shortcuts that SSC uses again and again (O is where the two lines meet):

What meets at O∠BOC
Internal bisectors of ∠B and ∠C (O is the incentre)90° + ∠A/2
External bisectors of ∠B and ∠C90° − ∠A/2
Internal bisector of ∠B and external bisector of ∠C∠A/2
Altitudes from B and C (O is the orthocentre)180° − ∠A
O is the circumcentre (acute triangle)2∠A

Also: the angle between the bisector of ∠A and the altitude from A is |∠B − ∠C|/2.

Example: internal bisectors of ∠B and ∠C meet at O and ∠BOC = 122°. Then 90° + ∠A/2 = 122°, so ∠A = 64°.

concepts.title: Congruence and similarity
concepts.body:
Congruent triangles have the same shape and size. Tests: SSS, SAS (the angle must be between the two sides), ASA, AAS, and RHS (right angle, hypotenuse, one side). SSA and AAA do not prove congruence. Matching parts of congruent triangles are equal (CPCT).

Similar triangles have the same shape. Tests: AA (two equal angles), SSS (all sides in the same ratio), SAS (two sides in the same ratio and the angle between them equal).

If two triangles are similar with side ratio k:

  • Perimeters, altitudes, medians, angle bisectors and inradii are all in ratio k.
  • Areas are in ratio k2. So areas 196 : 625 give sides √196 : √625 = 14 : 25. Altitudes 2 : 5 give areas 4 : 25.

Basic proportionality theorem (BPT): if DE ∥ BC in ΔABC (D on AB, E on AC), then AD/DB = AE/EC, and ΔADE is similar to ΔABC with ratio AD/AB. The converse is also true: if the sides are cut in the same ratio, DE ∥ BC.

Midpoint theorem: the line joining the midpoints of two sides is parallel to the third side and half of it. Joining all three midpoints makes 4 equal triangles, each 1/4 of the area.

Same height, area in ratio of bases: triangles with the same apex and bases on one line have areas in the ratio of their bases. A median splits a triangle into two equal areas. Example: P on BC with BP : PC = 4 : 11 and Q the midpoint of BP. Then BQ = 2/15 of BC, so ar(ABQ) : ar(ABC) = 2 : 15.

concepts.title: Angle bisector, median and Apollonius
concepts.body:
Use a = BC, b = CA, c = AB.

  • Angle bisector theorem: if AD bisects ∠A, then BD/DC = AB/AC = c/b. So BD = ac/(b + c) and DC = ab/(b + c).
  • The external bisector of ∠A divides BC externally in the same ratio c : b.
  • Apollonius theorem: if AD is the median to BC, then AB2 + AC2 = 2(AD2 + BD2).
  • Median length: AD = ½√(2b2 + 2c2 − a2).
  • Sum of the squares of the three medians = ¾ (a2 + b2 + c2).
  • In a right triangle, the median to the hypotenuse is half the hypotenuse.

Example 1: sides 6, 7 and 8 cm. The largest angle faces the side 8 cm and sits between 6 and 7. Its bisector cuts the 8 cm side into 8 × 6/13 = 48/13 ≈ 3.69 cm and 8 × 7/13 = 56/13 ≈ 4.31 cm.

Example 2: AB = 6, AC = 8, BC = 10. Median AD = ½√(72 + 128 − 100) = ½√100 = 5 (the triangle is right-angled, so it is also half of 10).

concepts.title: Triangle centres
concepts.body:
CentreWhere the lines meetFacts to remember
Centroid GMedians (vertex to midpoint of opposite side)Cuts each median 2 : 1 from the vertex (AG : GD = 2 : 1). The three medians make 6 small triangles of equal area. ar(BGC) = ar(AGB) = ⅓ ar(ABC); ar(BDG) = ⅙ ar(ABC). Always inside.
Incentre IInternal angle bisectorsSame distance r from all three sides; centre of the incircle. r = Area/s, where s = half the perimeter. ∠BIC = 90° + ∠A/2. Always inside.
Circumcentre OPerpendicular bisectors of the sidesSame distance R from all three vertices; centre of the circumcircle. R = abc/(4 × Area). ∠BOC = 2∠A for an acute triangle. Inside for acute, at the midpoint of the hypotenuse for right (R = hypotenuse/2), outside for obtuse.
Orthocentre HAltitudes∠BHC = 180° − ∠A. Inside for acute, at the right-angle corner for right, outside for obtuse.
  • In an equilateral triangle all four centres are the same point.
  • In an isosceles triangle all four lie on the axis of symmetry.
  • Euler line: O, G and H lie on one line, with G between them and HG = 2 GO.
  • Three points on one straight line (like 9 cm, 11 cm, 20 cm apart: 9 + 11 = 20) have no circle through them. Any three non-collinear points have exactly one.

Example: ∠A = 68° and I is the incentre. ∠BIC = 90° + 34° = 124°.

concepts.title: Incircle and tangent lengths
concepts.body:
The two tangents from a vertex to the incircle are equal. In the figure AR = AQ = x, BR = BP = y, CP = CQ = z, so the perimeter is 2(x + y + z).

  • With s = (a + b + c)/2: tangent length from A = s − a, from B = s − b, from C = s − c.
  • Inradius r = Area/s. Area = r × s.
  • Right triangle with legs a, b and hypotenuse c: r = (a + b − c)/2, R = c/2.
  • Excircle: if a circle touches side BC and sides AB and AC extended, the tangent length from A to it equals s, half the perimeter of ΔABC.
  • A quadrilateral with a circle touching all four sides: AB + CD = AD + BC (opposite sides add up equally).

Example 1: AB = 16, BC = 20, AC = 24. s = 30. Tangent from A = 30 − 20 = 10, from B = 30 − 24 = 6, from C = 30 − 16 = 14.

Example 2: right triangle with legs 5 and 12, hypotenuse 13. r = (5 + 12 − 13)/2 = 2.

Example 3: AB = 18, BC = 21, AD = 15 and a circle touches all four sides. CD = AD + BC − AB = 15 + 21 − 18 = 18.

concepts.title: Pythagoras and the type of triangle
concepts.body:
In a right triangle, hypotenuse2 = sum of squares of the other two sides.

Learn these triplets (and their multiples, like 6-8-10 and 9-12-15):

TripletTriplet
3, 4, 520, 21, 29
5, 12, 139, 40, 41
8, 15, 1712, 35, 37
7, 24, 2511, 60, 61

Make more with m > n: (m2 − n2, 2mn, m2 + n2).

Acute, right or obtuse? Let c be the longest side. If c2 < a2 + b2 the triangle is acute; if equal, right; if greater, obtuse. Example: 7, 24, 30. 302 = 900 and 72 + 242 = 625, so it is obtuse.

Altitude on the hypotenuse: in ΔABC with ∠A = 90° and AD ⊥ BC:

  • AD = AB × AC / BC
  • BD = AB2/BC and CD = AC2/BC
  • AD2 = BD × DC

Example: AB = 12, AC = 16. BC = 20, AD = 192/20 = 9.6, BD = 144/20 = 7.2, CD = 256/20 = 12.8.

If a triangle inscribed in a circle has sides 20, 21, 29, it is right-angled (400 + 441 = 841), so the circumradius is 29/2 = 14.5.

concepts.title: Special triangles
concepts.body:
TriangleSides
30°-60°-90°1 : √3 : 2 (short side faces 30°, hypotenuse is twice it)
45°-45°-90°1 : 1 : √2

Equilateral triangle with side a:

QuantityFormula
Height (also median, bisector)√3a/2
Area√3a2/4
Inradius ra/(2√3) = height/3
Circumradius Ra/√3 = 2 × height/3
R : r2 : 1

Examples: side 24 cm gives r = 24/(2√3) = 4√3 ≈ 6.93 cm. Side 36 cm gives R = 36/√3 = 12√3 cm. If the circumcentre is 3.2 cm from the base, that distance is r, so the height is 3 × 3.2 = 9.6 cm.

Isosceles triangle: the altitude to the base bisects the base and the top angle.

concepts.title: Chords of a circle
concepts.body:
• The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord. With radius r, distance d and chord length L: r2 = d2 + (L/2)2.
  • Equal chords are equally far from the centre, and the other way round. A chord nearer the centre is longer.
  • The diameter is the longest chord. So if a chord is 20.5 cm, the radius is at least 10.25 cm.
  • Equal chords make equal angles at the centre.
  • Concentric circles (radii R > r): a chord of the big circle that touches the small one has length 2√(R2 − r2). Radii 26 and 10 give 2√576 = 48.
  • Common chord of two intersecting circles is perpendicular to the line joining the centres and is bisected by it.

Example: chord of 16 cm at 6 cm from the centre. r = √(36 + 64) = 10 cm.

Example (common chord): radii 15 and 13, centres 14 apart. Let the chord be x from the first centre: 152 − x2 = 132 − (14 − x)2 gives x = 9. Half-chord = √(225 − 81) = 12, so the chord is 24.

concepts.title: Angles in a circle
concepts.body:
• The angle an arc makes at the centre is twice the angle it makes anywhere on the rest of the circle.
  • Angles in the same segment (standing on the same arc, same side) are equal.
  • The angle in a semicircle is 90°.
  • An angle in the major segment is acute; an angle in the minor segment is obtuse. The two add to 180°.
  • In ΔAOB with O the centre, OA = OB, so ∠OAB = ∠OBA = (180° − ∠AOB)/2.

Example: P is on the minor arc and ∠APB = 122°. A point on the major arc sees AB at 180° − 122° = 58°, so ∠AOB = 116° and ∠OAB = (180° − 116°)/2 = 32°.

Chord and inscribed angle: chord AB = 2R sin C, where C is the angle on the circle. A 10 cm chord seen at 30° from the major arc gives R = 10/(2 × ½) = 10 cm.

concepts.title: Cyclic quadrilaterals
concepts.body:
A quadrilateral with all four corners on a circle is cyclic.

  • Opposite angles add to 180°: ∠A + ∠C = ∠B + ∠D = 180°.
  • An exterior angle equals the opposite interior angle.
  • If one side is a diameter, the angles standing on it are 90°.
  • Ptolemy (for advanced questions): AC × BD = AB × CD + AD × BC.
  • A parallelogram that is cyclic must be a rectangle. A cyclic trapezium is isosceles.

Example: ∠A = 67°, ∠B = 92°. ∠C = 113°, ∠D = 88°, so ∠C − ∠D = 25°.

Example: AB is a diameter and ∠ADC = 145°. ∠ABC = 180° − 145° = 35° and ∠ACB = 90°, so ∠BAC = 55°.

concepts.title: Tangents and common tangents
concepts.body:
• A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. Tangent length from a point at distance d from the centre = √(d2 − r2).
  • The two tangents from an outside point P are equal (PA = PB), PO bisects ∠APB, and ∠APB + ∠AOB = 180°.
  • Alternate segment theorem: the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle the chord makes in the other segment.
  • If chord AB has length L at distance d from the centre, the tangents at A and B meet at T with TA = r × (L/2)/d. Chord 32, radius 20: d = 12, so TA = 20 × 16/12 ≈ 26.67.

Two circles with radii r1, r2 and centres d apart:

  • Direct common tangent = √(d2 − (r1 − r2)2)
  • Transverse common tangent = √(d2 − (r1 + r2)2)
Position of the circlesCommon tangents
Apart (d > r1 + r2)4
Touching outside (d = r1 + r2)3
Cutting at two points2
Touching inside (d = r1 − r2)1
One inside the other, not touching0

Example: radii 2 and 6, centres 5 apart. Direct tangent = √(25 − 16) = 3. Radii 5 and 10, centres 17 apart. Transverse tangent = √(289 − 225) = 8.

concepts.title: Chord and secant products
concepts.body:
• Intersecting chords: if chords AB and CD meet at P inside the circle, PA × PB = PC × PD.
  • Two secants from an outside point P: PA × PB = PC × PD (whole lengths measured from P).
  • Tangent and secant: if TP is a tangent and TQR a secant, TP2 = TQ × TR.

Example: AP = 6, PB = 8, CP = 4. PD = 48/4 = 12.

Example: tangent TP = 12, TQ = x, TR = x + 7. x(x + 7) = 144 gives x = 9.

concepts.title: Quadrilaterals
concepts.body:
The angles of any quadrilateral add to 360°.

ShapeKey facts
ParallelogramOpposite sides equal and parallel; opposite angles equal; neighbouring angles add to 180°; diagonals bisect each other; d12 + d22 = 2(a2 + b2).
RectangleParallelogram with 90° angles; diagonals equal.
RhombusAll sides equal; diagonals bisect each other at 90° and bisect the angles; side = ½√(d12 + d22).
SquareRectangle and rhombus together; diagonal = side × √2.
TrapeziumOne pair of parallel sides; the line joining midpoints of the other two sides = (sum of parallel sides)/2; diagonals cut each other in the ratio of the parallel sides.
KiteTwo pairs of equal neighbouring sides; the main diagonal is an axis of symmetry and cuts the other diagonal at 90°.
  • Joining the midpoints of any quadrilateral gives a parallelogram (of a rectangle, a rhombus; of a rhombus, a rectangle).
  • If the bisectors of ∠C and ∠D meet at E, then ∠CED = (∠A + ∠B)/2.

Example: in trapezium ABCD (AB ∥ DC), diagonals meet at P with AP = 3x − 1, PC = 5x − 3, BP = 2x + 1, PD = 6x − 5. AP/PC = BP/PD gives 2x2 − 5x + 2 = 0, so x = 2 (x = ½ makes PC negative).

concepts.title: Polygons
concepts.body:
For a polygon with n sides:

  • Sum of interior angles = (n − 2) × 180°.
  • Sum of exterior angles = 360° (any convex polygon).
  • Regular polygon: each exterior angle = 360°/n, each interior angle = 180° − 360°/n. So n = 360°/exterior angle.
  • Number of diagonals = n(n − 3)/2.
  • A regular hexagon is 6 equilateral triangles: area = 3√3a2/2.
Sides nInterior angle sumEach interior angleEach exterior angleDiagonals
5540°108°72°5
6720°120°60°9
81080°135°45°20
91260°140°40°27
101440°144°36°35
121800°150°30°54
152340°156°24°90
182880°160°20°135
203240°162°18°170

Example: interior angles of a hexagon and a 12-sided polygon are 120° and 150°, a ratio of 4 : 5.

varieties.name: Angles in triangles and lines
varieties.how: Write the angle sum (180°) or the exterior angle rule for each triangle in the figure. When bisectors, altitudes or extended sides meet, use the shortcut table: 90° + A/2, 90° − A/2, A/2 or 180° − A.

example.q: In ΔABC, ∠B = 72° and ∠C = 44°. BC is extended to D. The bisectors of ∠ABC and ∠ACD meet at E. Find ∠BEC.
steps: E is where an internal bisector (of ∠B) meets an external bisector (of ∠C), so ∠BEC = ∠A/2.

varieties.name: Congruence, similarity and proportion
varieties.how: Find the pair of similar triangles (look for parallel lines or two equal angles), write the side ratio k, then use k for lengths and k<sup>2</sup> for areas.

example.q: In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC with D on AB and E on AC. If AD : DB = 2 : 3, find the ratio of the area of ΔADE to the area of trapezium DBCE.
steps: ΔADE is similar to ΔABC with AD/AB = 2/(2 + 3) = 2/5.
Area ratio = (2/5)<sup>2</sup> = 4/25. So ΔADE = 4 parts and ΔABC = 25 parts.

varieties.name: Triangle centres and medians
varieties.how: Name the centre first: medians give the centroid (2 : 1, equal areas), angle bisectors give the incentre (90° + A/2, r = Area/s), perpendicular bisectors give the circumcentre (2A, R = abc/4Area), altitudes give the orthocentre (180° − A).

example.q: In ΔABC, ∠A = 68° and I is the incentre. Find ∠BIC.
steps: The incentre is where the internal angle bisectors meet.

varieties.name: Pythagoras and special triangles
varieties.how: Look for a triplet first (3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, 20-21-29). With a perpendicular from the right angle to the hypotenuse, use BD = AB<sup>2</sup>/BC and AD = AB × AC/BC. For 30° and 45° angles use 1 : √3 : 2 and 1 : 1 : √2.

example.q: In ΔABC, ∠A = 90° and AD ⊥ BC. If AB = 12 cm and AC = 16 cm, find BD.

varieties.name: Chords and angles in circles
varieties.how: Mark the centre and every 90° angle (semicircle, perpendicular to a chord). Use centre angle = 2 × angle on the circle, and opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°. For chord lengths, use r<sup>2</sup> = d<sup>2</sup> + (L/2)<sup>2</sup>.

example.q: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral, AB is a diameter of the circle and ∠ADC = 145°. Find ∠BAC.
steps: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral: ∠ABC = 180° − 145° = 35°.
AB is a diameter, so ∠ACB = 90° (angle in a semicircle).

varieties.name: Tangents and secants
varieties.how: Join the centre to the point of contact to get a right angle, then use Pythagoras. For two circles use √(d<sup>2</sup> − (r<sub>1</sub> − r<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup>) for the direct tangent and √(d<sup>2</sup> − (r<sub>1</sub> + r<sub>2</sub>)<sup>2</sup>) for the transverse one. For a tangent and a secant, TP<sup>2</sup> = TQ × TR.

example.q: The radii of two circles are 6 cm and 2 cm and their centres are 10 cm apart. Find the length of a transverse common tangent.

varieties.name: Quadrilaterals
varieties.how: Use the angle sum 360° and the property of the named shape (diagonals of a rhombus meet at 90°, diagonals of a trapezium cut in the ratio of the parallel sides, and so on).

example.q: In quadrilateral ABCD, the bisectors of ∠C and ∠D meet at E. If ∠CED = 57° and ∠A = 47°, find ∠B.

varieties.name: Regular polygons
varieties.how: Get n from the exterior angle (n = 360°/exterior angle), or from the interior angle via exterior = 180° − interior. Then use (n − 2) × 180° for the angle sum and n(n − 3)/2 for diagonals.

example.q: The exterior angle of a regular polygon is 18°. How many diagonals does it have?

tips: Draw a rough figure every time and mark the right angles first: angle in a semicircle, radius to tangent, centre to the midpoint of a chord, altitude.
Learn the triplets 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25 and 20-21-29 with their multiples; they hide in most length questions.
For angle questions where bisectors or altitudes meet, use the shortcuts 90° + A/2, 90° − A/2, A/2 and 180° − A instead of chasing every angle.
Similar triangles: lengths go with k, areas go with k<sup>2</sup>. Write both ratios before you calculate.
Area ratio questions inside one triangle: triangles with the same height have areas in the ratio of their bases, and a median halves the area.
In an equilateral triangle, inradius : circumradius : height = 1 : 2 : 3.
Use common sense to cut options: an obtuse angle cannot be 40°, and no chord is longer than the diameter.
traps: The centre angle is twice the angle on the circle only when both stand on the same arc. A point on the minor arc sees the chord at 180° minus the major-arc angle.
In the bisector shortcuts, check whether the bisectors are internal or external: 90° + A/2 and 90° − A/2 are easy to swap.
Area ratio of similar triangles is the square of the side ratio, not the side ratio itself.
SSA and AAA do not prove congruence; AAA only proves similarity.
Direct common tangent uses r<sub>1</sub> − r<sub>2</sub>; transverse uses r<sub>1</sub> + r<sub>2</sub>.
Sum of exterior angles is 360° for every polygon; do not use (n − 2) × 180° for exterior angles.

questions.q: In the given figure, ∠BAC = 50° and ∠ABC = 70°. Side BC is extended to D. What is ∠ACD?
In the given figure, AB is a diameter of the circle with centre O and C is a point on the circle. If ∠CAB = 35°, what is ∠CBA?
In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC with D on AB and E on AC. If AD = 4 cm, DB = 6 cm and AE = 6 cm, find EC.
questions.solution:
By the Basic Proportionality Theorem, AD/DB = AE/EC.
4/6 = 6/EC → EC = 36/4 = 9 cm.

questions.q: A point P is 13 cm from the centre O of a circle of radius 5 cm. What is the length of the tangent PT drawn from P to the circle?
In the given figure, O is the centre of the circle and ∠AOB = 110°. C is a point on the major arc. What is ∠ACB?
questions.solution:
The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc AB.
∠ACB = 110°/2 = 55°.

questions.q: In ΔABC, AD is the bisector of ∠A meeting BC at D. If AB = 6 cm, AC = 9 cm and BC = 10 cm, find BD.
questions.solution:
Angle bisector theorem: BD/DC = AB/AC = 6/9 = 2/3.
BD = 10 × 2/(2 + 3) = 4 cm.
